introduction_markdown: CAMEROON GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination / Technical and Vocational Education Examination. 0785 Religious Studies 1, JUNE 2020, ADVANCED LEVEL. Multiple choice question paper, one and a half hours. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Instructions to candidates: read the instructions carefully before you start answering the questions; make sure you have a soft HB pencil and an eraser for this examination. Use a soft HB pencil throughout the examination. Do not open this booklet until you are told to do so. Before the examination begins, check that the question booklet is headed 'Advanced Level - 0785 Religious Studies 1'; fill in the information required in the spaces above and on the answer sheet using your HB pencil (Candidate Name, Exam Session, Subject Code and Candidate Identification Number), taking care not to crease or fold the answer sheet or to make any marks on it other than those asked for. Answer ALL the 50 questions in this examination; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is appropriate, find the number of the question on the answer sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square brackets for the answer you have chosen (for example, if C is your correct answer, mark C). Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you will score a zero for that question; if you change your mind about an answer, erase the first mark carefully, then mark your new answer. Avoid spending too much time on any one question: if you find a question difficult, move on to the next question and come back to it later. Do all rough work in this booklet using the blank spaces in the question booklet. At the end of the examination the invigilator shall collect the answer sheet first and then the question booklet; do not attempt to leave the examination hall with it.

questions.enonce_markdown: One of the signs of the covenant with Abraham was:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Genesis 17 God makes a covenant with Abraham and gives circumcision as its outward sign ("the sign of the covenant"). The blessing, the many descendants and the gift of the land are the promises of the covenant, not the sign by which the covenant was marked on the body of every male in Abraham's household.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown:
How did Jacob usurp his brother's rights to inheritance as the first born son?

*Options as printed:* A) By the help of Rebecca   B) By providing a meal   C) By escaping to Haran   D) By preparing meat for his father
questions.corrige_markdown:
Esau, the elder twin, was the first born son. In Genesis 25 he came in from the field very hungry and Jacob gave him a meal of stew in exchange for his birthright, the rights of the first born, which Esau accepted. This is the most direct way in which Jacob took the first born's inheritance rights. The later story of the blessing (Genesis 27) is different: there it was Rebekah who prepared the meat for Isaac and helped Jacob to deceive his father, so options A and D describe the stealing of the blessing (a reading that also makes option A defensible), and option C (his flight to Haran) happened afterwards, to escape Esau's anger.

**Intended answer: B (By providing a meal).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: How many sons did Jacob have?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Jacob had twelve sons (Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph and Benjamin), the ancestors of the twelve tribes of Israel. He also had at least one daughter, Dinah; counting all his children gives thirteen, which is the trap in option C, but the question asks about sons.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: Where was Jacob's name modified?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Genesis 32 Jacob wrestled with a mysterious man at the ford of the Jabbok and was told: "Your name shall no more be called Jacob, but Israel." Jacob called the place Peniel (or Penuel), "the face of God". Bethel (formerly Luz) is where Jacob had his dream of the ladder, and the new name is repeated there in Genesis 35, but the change of name is traditionally placed at Peniel. Haran is where Jacob lived with Laban.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: Where did Joseph's family settle in Egypt?
questions.corrige_markdown:
After Joseph revealed himself to his brothers, Pharaoh gave Jacob's household the land of Goshen in the Nile delta, good pasture land (Genesis 45 to 47). Memphis was an Egyptian city, Haran is in Mesopotamia and is where Abraham's family had lived earlier, and Sinai is the wilderness mountain where Israel received the Law after leaving Egypt.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: God first appeared to Moses in the form of:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Exodus 3 Moses, tending Jethro's flock near Horeb, saw a bush that burned without being consumed, and God spoke to him from it and called him to lead Israel out of Egypt. The pillar of cloud and fire and the smoke on Mount Sinai came later in the story.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown: Moses used this object to demonstrate Yahweh's power:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Moses' shepherd's staff was the sign of God's power: it became a snake before Pharaoh, was used in the plagues, and was stretched out over the sea and struck on the rock (Exodus 4, 7 and 14, 17). The stone tablets carried the Law, not a demonstration of power. The Bible does not describe the staff as bronze or iron.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown:
What did God provide for the Israelites in the desert?

*Options as printed:* A) Fish   B) Manna   C) Leeks   D) Meat
questions.corrige_markdown:
The food that God provided every morning during the forty years in the wilderness was manna (Exodus 16). However, the Bible also says that God sent quails, that is meat, to the camp (Exodus 16 and Numbers 11), so option D is also defensible. Fish and leeks were foods that the people remembered from Egypt (Numbers 11:5); they were not provided in the desert. The expected answer is manna, but because two options can be defended the question is left open.

**Intended answer: B (Manna).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown: Why did Moses break the stone tablets at the foot of Mount Sinai?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Exodus 32 Moses came down from the mountain, saw the people dancing around the golden calf that Aaron had made, and in his anger threw down the tablets and broke them. The immediate reason is the worship of the golden calf. Option B describes what the broken tablets symbolised (the people had broken the covenant), but it is the consequence of the idolatry rather than the reason for the act. Moses was angry with the people, not with God, and Aaron had not taken over the leadership.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown: For how long did the Israelites wander in the desert?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Because the people refused to enter the promised land after the report of the spies, they wandered in the wilderness for forty years until that generation had died (Numbers 14, Deuteronomy 8). "Forty days" is the length of Moses' stay on the mountain, which is the trap in option A.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown: Joshua warned the Israelites not to:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In his farewell speeches (Joshua 23 and 24) Joshua warned Israel not to mix with the nations that remained in the land, not to intermarry with them and not to serve their gods, for this would lead them away from the Lord. The other options are not warnings: Joshua himself led the crossing of the Jordan and divided the land among the tribes.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - joshua and the conquest

choix.texte: Harvest grapes from the conquered land
Divide the Land among the twelve
Cross the Jordan to other side

questions.enonce_markdown: Why did God reject Saul as the king in Israel?
questions.corrige_markdown:
According to 1 Samuel 13 and 15, Saul disobeyed God's commands: he offered the sacrifice himself instead of waiting for Samuel, and he spared King Agag and the best of the animals of the Amalekites against the instruction given to him. Samuel told him that to obey is better than sacrifice, and that the Lord had rejected him as king. His jealousy and attempts against David came after this rejection, and it was the people, not Saul, who had asked for a king.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

He did not want Israel to have a king

questions.enonce_markdown: Prophet Nathan rebuked David because:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In 2 Samuel 11 and 12 David took Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and arranged for Uriah to die in battle. The prophet Nathan told him the parable of the rich man and the poor man's lamb and said "You are the man". Moving the capital to Jerusalem was not condemned, and the census of the people is a different episode (2 Samuel 24) in which the prophet Gad was involved.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy
A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: What important religious symbol did the Philistines return to Israel during the reign of David?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Philistines had captured the Ark of the Covenant, the sacred chest that was the symbol of God's presence, and sent it back to Israel after misfortunes struck them (1 Samuel 4 to 6). David later brought the Ark to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). The Ark is the only option that matches this episode. (In the biblical account the return by the Philistines comes before David's reign, but the object is clearly the Ark.)

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown:
How did Absalom compromise his brief overthrow of David?

*Options as printed:* A) By gathering young men behind him   B) By killing the Priests of Israel   C) By taunting David and his army as they fled from Jerusalem   D) By dividing the kingdom into two
questions.corrige_markdown:
In 2 Samuel 15 to 18 Absalom took Jerusalem and David fled across the Jordan. Absalom's coup failed mainly because he rejected the advice of Ahithophel to pursue David at once and followed the delaying advice of Hushai, David's friend, which gave David time to regroup. None of the four printed options states this clearly, and the options do not match the biblical account (Absalom did not kill the priests or divide the kingdom). The key of the printed paper cannot be established with certainty, so the question is left open for self-assessment.

Model answer: Absalom compromised his own revolt by accepting Hushai's advice to delay and gather all Israel instead of attacking David immediately, so David escaped, reorganised his forces and defeated Absalom's army.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: What event triggered the division of Israel into two kingdoms?
questions.corrige_markdown:
After Solomon's death the northern tribes, with Jeroboam as their spokesman, asked Rehoboam to lighten the heavy labour and taxes imposed by Solomon. Rehoboam refused and answered harshly, and the northern tribes broke away to form the kingdom of Israel while Judah stayed with the house of David (1 Kings 12). Option B, a disagreement between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, is the only option close to this event. Jeroboam set up the shrines at Bethel and Dan after the division, the Assyrians conquered Israel much later (722 BCE), and it was the northern tribes, not Rehoboam, who seceded.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

choix.texte: Jeroboam desecrated the Temple in Jerusalem
Rehoboam did not agree with Jeroboam
The Assyrians were too powerful for Israel

questions.enonce_markdown: Who was Elisha in relation to Elijah?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Elijah was told to anoint Elisha as prophet in his place (1 Kings 19). Elisha followed Elijah as his servant and, when Elijah was taken up, he received his mantle and a share of his spirit (2 Kings 2). He was therefore Elijah's successor.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: What did the death of King Ahab and his wife, Jezebel have in common?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Ahab was wounded in battle at Ramoth Gilead and died in his chariot; when the chariot was washed at the pool of Samaria the dogs licked his blood (1 Kings 22). Jezebel was thrown from a window on Jehu's orders and the dogs ate her body (2 Kings 9). Both deaths were seen as the fulfilment of Elijah's prophecy about the house of Ahab (1 Kings 21), and dogs feature in both. Only Ahab died in battle, and no Philistines or angel stabbing are involved.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

choix.texte: The angel of God stabbed them in sleep
The Philistines took out their eyes

questions.enonce_markdown: Who is the first prophet in Islam?
questions.corrige_markdown:
According to Islamic tradition, Adam was the first human being and also the first prophet, and the line of prophets continued through Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and others to Muhammad. Ibrahim, Ishmael and Yakub (Jacob) came much later in that line.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets in islam

questions.enonce_markdown: The last and final prophet in Islam is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Muslims believe that Muhammad is the last of the prophets, the "Seal of the Prophets", and that the Qur'an revealed to him is God's final message. Yakub (Jacob), Isa (Jesus) and Daud (David) are earlier prophets in Islamic belief.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets in islam

questions.enonce_markdown:
How many prophets are mentioned in the Holy Qur'an by name?

*Options as printed:* A) 160   B) 40   C) 60   D) 24
questions.corrige_markdown:
Islamic tradition usually says that twenty five prophets are named in the Qur'an, from Adam to Muhammad, although some lists give a slightly different count (for example 24 or 26) depending on which figures are counted as prophets. None of the printed options is the usual figure of twenty five (24 is the nearest), so the key cannot be fixed with confidence and the question is left open for self-assessment.

Model answer: about twenty five prophets are named in the Qur'an, among them Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets in islam

questions.enonce_markdown: In which year did the Islamic calendar begin?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Islamic (Hijri) calendar counts its years from the Hijra, the migration of the Prophet Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina, which took place in 622 CE. The year 570 CE is the traditional date of the Prophet's birth, which is the trap in option A.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: The Holiest month in Islam is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, is the month of the obligatory fast (sawm), the month in which Muslims believe the Qur'an began to be revealed, and is generally regarded as the holiest month. Dhul Hijja is the month of the Hajj and is also sacred, but it is not regarded as the holiest; options A and C are two spellings of that same month. Sha'ban is the month before Ramadan.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown: How is Zakat on one's income calculated in Islam?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Zakat, the third pillar of Islam, is the obligatory yearly giving to the needy. The usual rate on savings and qualifying wealth above the minimum threshold (nisab) is one fortieth, that is 2.5 per cent. The other percentages are not the standard rate for this kind of wealth.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown: This food is considered as haram in Islam:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Haram means forbidden. The Qur'an forbids the eating of pork, and Muslims avoid it, as well as the meat of animals not slaughtered in the proper way. Fish, beef and mutton are halal (permitted) when properly prepared.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic scriptures and law

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these is recommended for women in Islam?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Islamic teaching asks both men and women to dress modestly, and for women this is traditionally expressed by covering the hair and body, that is by wearing the veil or headscarf (the hijab). Among the printed options the veil is the item expected as the answer; trousers, gowns and blouses are ordinary garments that are not in themselves the specific Islamic recommendation.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - women in islam
A Level Religious Studies - islamic scriptures and law

questions.enonce_markdown: Muhammad's final Sermon to his disciples was delivered on:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Farewell Sermon was given by the Prophet during his last pilgrimage to Mecca, at Mount Arafat (Arafah), on the ninth day of Dhul Hijja. Mount Sinai is linked with Moses, Mount Carmel with Elijah and Mount Moriah with Abraham and the Jerusalem Temple.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: The Muslim Hajj has as destination the holy city of:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Hajj, the fifth pillar of Islam, is the pilgrimage to Mecca (Makkah), where the Ka'ba stands. Arafat is a place near Mecca visited during the rites of the pilgrimage, but it is not a city. Medina is often visited but is not the destination of the Hajj, and Jerusalem is a holy city for Muslims but not the goal of the pilgrimage.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown: The holiest and most sacred object in Islam is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Muslims regard the Qur'an as the word of God (Allah) revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, and treat the book with great reverence. Prayer beads, the dress of the hijab and the Dome (a building) are not regarded as the most sacred object.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic scriptures and law

questions.enonce_markdown: The prophet in Islam who is returning to complete his mission is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
According to Islamic tradition (the hadith), Isa ibn Maryam, that is Jesus son of Mary, will return towards the end of time to establish justice and to oppose the false messiah (the Dajjal). Muhammad, Musa (Moses) and Ibrahim (Abraham) are not expected to return in this way. Christians and Muslims understand the figure of Jesus differently, and this answer reflects the Islamic teaching only.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets in islam

questions.enonce_markdown: The Buddha delivered his first sermon, known as 'Turning of the wheel of law' at:
questions.corrige_markdown:
After his enlightenment the Buddha went to the Deer Park at Sarnath, near Varanasi, and preached to his first five disciples the sermon known as the setting in motion of the wheel of the Dharma (the Turning of the wheel of law), which includes the Four Noble Truths. Bodh Gaya is the place of the enlightenment, and Sanchi is known for its stupa.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: Where is Lumbini, the birth place of Gautama Buddha located?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lumbini, where Siddhartha Gautama was born, is in southern Nepal, near the border with India. Bihar is the Indian state of Bodh Gaya, and Bhutan and Sikkim are Himalayan regions that are not the birthplace.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown:
Where did Buddha attain Nirvana?

*Options as printed:* A) Bodh Gaya   B) Kushinagara   C) Rajgriha   D) Vaishali
questions.corrige_markdown:
Buddhist tradition says that Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment (bodhi, often called Nirvana) under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, and this is the answer usually expected. However, the Buddha's death, called parinirvana (final Nirvana), took place at Kushinagara, so option B can also be defended depending on how the word Nirvana is understood. For this reason the question is left open for self-assessment.

**Intended answer: A (Bodh Gaya).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: The process of retribution in Buddhism is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Karma is the law by which intentional actions, good or bad, have consequences for the person who performs them, in this life and in future rebirths. Nirvana is liberation from the cycle of rebirth, the Vedas are the oldest Hindu scriptures and yoga is a discipline of body and mind.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown:
The best known book of the Hindu Scripture is?

*Options as printed:* A) Ramayana   B) Vedas   C) Bragavad Vila   D) Sanskrit
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hindu scripture includes the Vedas (the oldest and most authoritative texts, the shruti), the epics such as the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, and the Bhagavad Gita, which is the text most widely read and quoted (the printed option C "Bragavad Vila" is a misspelling of it). Sanskrit is a language, not a book. The words "best known" do not allow one single option to be chosen with confidence (the Vedas or the Bhagavad Gita), so the question is left open for self-assessment.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: A Hindu is essentially a:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hindu teaching stresses ahimsa, non-violence towards living beings, and many Hindus follow a vegetarian diet; for this reason the expected answer is vegetarian. Practice varies among Hindus and regions, and the word "essentially" is a generalisation. "Herbivorous" describes animals that eat only plants, and carnivorous and pescatarian are not the traditional ideal.

**Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: A sacred animal in Hinduism is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The cow is the animal most widely revered in Hinduism, as a symbol of motherhood, generosity and non-violence, and the eating of beef is avoided by most Hindus. The elephant is also honoured, notably through the god Ganesha, but the cow is the sacred animal that is expected as the answer.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: Jews consider Abraham as their:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Abraham, with Isaac and Jacob, is regarded in Judaism as one of the patriarchs, the founding fathers of the Jewish people, with whom God made the covenant. He is also called a prophet in Genesis, but the title by which Jews honour him as ancestor of the nation is patriarch.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: The movement for the establishing of a Jewish state in Palestine during the 19th Century:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Zionism is the movement that aimed at the establishment of a Jewish homeland in Palestine. It became an organised political movement in the late 19th century, associated with Theodor Herzl and the First Zionist Congress at Basel (1897). Nazism and the Holocaust belong to the 20th century and are not movements for a Jewish state.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: The exposure of the Jews to the Greek culture is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hellenism is the spread of Greek language, ideas and customs after the conquests of Alexander the Great, to which the Jews, in Palestine and abroad, were exposed. Proselytism is the winning of converts, the Diaspora is the dispersion of the Jews outside Palestine and Zionism is the movement for a Jewish homeland.

**Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown:
An example of a bad death in ATR is:

*Options as printed:* A) Dying in a foreign land   B) Dying very young   C) Committing suicide   D) Dying in warfare
questions.corrige_markdown:
In many African traditional religions a good death comes at an old age, at home and surrounded by the family, while a bad death (by accident, drowning, in childbirth, by suicide, or far away from home) can prevent a person from joining the ancestors and requires special rites. Suicide is the example most commonly quoted, but dying young or in a foreign land is also considered a bad death in many societies, so several options can be defended and the question is left open for self-assessment. These are general beliefs, which vary among peoples.

**Intended answer: C (Committing suicide).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr death and ancestors

questions.enonce_markdown: The following are acts of worship in ATR except:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In ATR worship is expressed through rites such as sacrifices and offerings, prayers, festivals and the funeral and death ceremonies. Sowing seeds is an ordinary agricultural activity (even if it may be accompanied by a ritual) and is not itself an act of worship, so it is the exception. These are general descriptions, which vary among peoples.

**Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr worship and sacrifices

questions.enonce_markdown: The following are major places of worship in ATR except:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In ATR worship is typically offered at shrines, altars, sacred groves, rivers, hills and trees, and at places such as crossroads, rather than in large built temples of the kind found in other religions. Temples are therefore the expected exception. This is a generalisation, and some peoples do have shrine buildings.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The most powerful deity in ATR is (are):
questions.corrige_markdown:
In ATR the Supreme Being (called by different names among different peoples) is believed to be the creator and the highest power. The divinities act as his agents or ministers, and a soothsayer is a human diviner who has no such power.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr supreme being and divinities

questions.enonce_markdown: The "living dead" in ATR refers to:
questions.corrige_markdown:
"Living dead" is the term used by the scholar John Mbiti for ancestors: people who have died recently enough to be remembered by name by their living relatives, and who are believed to be still present, in the spirit world, and to watch over the family. Priests are living people, and spirits and deities are different beings.

**Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr death and ancestors

questions.enonce_markdown: ATR is the religion without:
questions.corrige_markdown:
African traditional religion has no founder and no written sacred scriptures. It is handed on orally, through myths, proverbs, songs, rituals and the example of elders. "Oral traditions" are exactly how it is transmitted, so that option cannot be the answer, and ATR does have living embodiments such as priests and elders.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: One of the attributes of the Supreme Being in ATR is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In ATR the Supreme Being is above all the creator of the world and of life, and many peoples also describe him as all-powerful, all-knowing and the source of life. Some traditions also speak of him as a judge who sees wrongdoing, but the attribute that is shared widely and expected is that of creator. The description "one with multiple eyes" is not a standard attribute.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
One of the major purposes of worship in ATR is:

*Options as printed:* A) To cleanse the land   B) To drive away the evil spirits   C) To appease the ancestors   D) Strengthening the link between the living and the Supreme Being
questions.corrige_markdown:
In ATR worship aims at keeping harmony between human beings and the spiritual world: thanking and asking help from the Supreme Being and the divinities, keeping good relations with the ancestors, protecting the community against evil forces and restoring the purity of the land after wrongdoing. Each of the four printed options is a purpose of worship in some tradition, and the question does not say which is the "major" one, so the key cannot be fixed with confidence and the question is left open for self-assessment. These are general beliefs, which vary among peoples.

questions.enonce_markdown: They occupy the highest positions and fall below God:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the usual description of the ATR hierarchy the Supreme Being is at the top, followed by the divinities (or the spirits and deities who serve him), then the ancestors, and then living human beings. Medicine-men and sorcerers are human beings. The divinities are therefore the beings who occupy the highest positions below God. (Ancestors also rank below God, but below the divinities.) This is a general scheme, which varies among peoples.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Time in ATR is determined by:

*Options as printed:* A) The length of the shadow   B) The event   C) The position of the sun   D) The crow of the cock
questions.corrige_markdown:
According to John Mbiti, time in traditional African thought is reckoned by events that have happened or are about to happen (birth, harvest, a festival, a death) rather than by abstract units of a clock. The shadow, the sun and the crow of the cock are practical ways of telling the time of day, so they can also be defended and the question is left open for self-assessment. This is a general view, which varies among peoples.

**Intended answer: B (The event).**
